title: Lyme Disease Serology: Two-Tier Testing, the 30-Day IgM Rule and Borrelia mayonii
summary: Learn how standard and modified two-tier Lyme serology work, the immunoblot band rules, why IgM blots count only in the first month, why early erythema migrans is diagnosed clinically, and how Borrelia mayonii differs.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 61 Hits 8 (standard two-tier), 9 (erythema migrans timing and frequency) and 14 (B. mayonii) and Exam Trap 5 (IgM blot beyond 4 weeks), checked against Moore 2016 (CDC review), Mead 2019 (MMWR), Branda & Steere 2021 (read via a page-fetch tool, first part of the article only), Pritt 2016 (read via a page-fetch tool), McGowan 2023 and Nafiz 2026. Qualifications: the reviewer’s “~40–60% sensitive in early disease” is higher than the acute-phase figures in the CDC review (about 30–40%; Branda 2021 cites 14% in solitary erythema migrans), and the modified two-tier test (CDC-accepted since 2019) is taught; B. mayonii is no longer only upper Midwest (New York 2025). Not taught: the reviewer’s “tick must feed >24–48 h” (Cook 2015 argues the minimum attachment time is not established), bull’s-eye frequency, and treatment.

objectives: Describe standard two-tier Lyme serology and the IgM and IgG immunoblot band criteria.
Apply the 30-day rule for IgM immunoblots and recognise that an isolated late IgM result may be a false positive.
Explain why erythema migrans with exposure is diagnosed clinically and what modified two-tier testing changes.
Recognise the clinical and laboratory clues of Borrelia mayonii infection.

scenes.title: Three Lyme requests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three Lyme disease requests arrive. (1) A hiker from an endemic area with a 7-cm expanding red patch 8 days after a tick bite; serology negative. (2) A patient with 8 weeks of knee swelling: IgM immunoblot positive, IgG immunoblot negative. (3) An acutely ill Minnesota woodcutter with high fever, patchy macular rash on the trunk and vomiting; serology negative. Question token: “Which result can you trust?”

cues.text: Three Lyme requests. A hiker with an expanding red patch eight days after a tick bite, and a negative antibody test. A patient with eight weeks of knee swelling.
The knee patient’s IgM blot is positive but the IgG blot is negative. A Minnesota woodcutter has high fever, a patchy rash and vomiting, with negative serology.
Which of these results can you trust, and which test was the wrong one?

scenes.title: Standard two-tier testing
scenes.altText: Schematic flow: tier 1 is a sensitive enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or immunofluorescence assay (IFA) for antibody to Borrelia burgdorferi. Negative stops there. Positive or equivocal reflexes to tier 2, a Western immunoblot. IgM blot positive = at least 2 of 3 bands (23 kDa OspC, 39, 41 kDa). IgG blot positive = at least 5 of 10 bands (18, 23, 28, 30, 39, 41, 45, 58, 66, 93 kDa). A warning card: the 41-kDa flagellin band cross-reacts with other bacterial flagella and was found in 43% of healthy controls in one study, so one IgM band or four or fewer IgG bands is not positive. Specificity of the full algorithm is above 95%.

cues.text: Standard Lyme serology has two tiers. First, a sensitive enzyme immunoassay, or an immunofluorescence assay. A negative result stops here.
A positive or equivocal first tier reflexes to a Western immunoblot, which looks for antibody to specific Borrelia proteins, shown as bands.
The IgM blot is positive with at least two of three bands. The IgG blot is positive with at least five of ten bands.

Fewer bands are not a positive result. The forty-one kilodalton flagellin band cross-reacts with other bacteria and is common in healthy people. Read correctly, the two tiers together are highly specific.

scenes.title: Timing decides the test
scenes.altText: Timeline card: tick bite → erythema migrans after about 1 week (range about 3–32 days) → IgM rises first → IgG follows. Rules card: IgM blot is reflexed together with IgG only when symptoms have lasted less than 30 days; beyond about a month most patients have IgG, so an IgM-only result should not be used as evidence of active disease and may be a false positive. Window-period card: in the acute phase of erythema migrans the standard two-tier test detects only a minority (about 30–40% in CDC-cited studies), so a patient with erythema migrans and endemic exposure is diagnosed clinically without testing. Modified two-tier card: since 2019, FDA-cleared assays may use a second EIA in place of the immunoblot; CDC accepts this as an alternative, and it is more sensitive in early disease.

cues.text: Timing decides which test means what. Erythema migrans, the expanding rash, appears about a week after the bite, with a range of roughly three days to a month. IgM antibody rises first, and IgG follows.

So the IgM blot counts only in the first thirty days of illness. After about a month, most patients have IgG, and an IgM-only result should not be used as evidence of active disease. It may well be a false positive.

Early on, antibodies lag. In the acute rash phase, two-tier testing is negative in most patients. That is why erythema migrans in someone with tick exposure in an endemic area is diagnosed clinically, without serology.
Since twenty nineteen, FDA-cleared kits may replace the immunoblot with a second enzyme immunoassay. CDC accepts this modified two-tier test, and it picks up more early cases.

scenes.title: Borrelia mayonii and the hook answers
scenes.altText: Card: Borrelia mayonii, described in 2016 from six patients in Minnesota, Wisconsin and North Dakota, carried by Ixodes scapularis. Median blood spirochete DNA load about 180 times that of B. burgdorferi; spirochetes seen by darkfield in one patient’s blood; fever 5 of 6, rash 4 of 6 (from diffuse macular to a single lesion), nausea or vomiting 4 of 6. High spirochetemia makes blood PCR useful before seroconversion. A 2025 New York case with infected local ticks extends the known range beyond the upper Midwest. Hook answers: (1) clinical erythema migrans, negative early serology expected; (2) 8 weeks with IgM-only blot: not evidence of active disease; (3) blood PCR for B. mayonii.

cues.text: A second Lyme species, Borrelia mayonii, was described in twenty sixteen from six patients in Minnesota, Wisconsin and North Dakota. Like Borrelia burgdorferi, it is carried by the blacklegged tick.

Its hallmark is unusually high spirochetemia: in that first report, a median blood DNA load about one hundred eighty times higher, with spirochetes seen in one patient’s blood. Most had fever, and most had nausea or vomiting; in at least two the rash was diffuse and macular, not erythema migrans.
Because so many spirochetes circulate, blood PCR can find it before antibodies appear. And in twenty twenty-five, a locally acquired case in New York showed it is not confined to the upper Midwest.

Back to the hook. The hiker has erythema migrans: a clinical diagnosis, and the negative serology is expected. The knee patient’s isolated IgM at eight weeks is not evidence of active Lyme disease. The woodcutter needs blood PCR for Borrelia mayonii.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Positive IgM blot at 8 weeks = active Lyme” (✓ after a month the IgM blot alone is not evidence of active disease); “One 41-kDa band = positive blot” (✓ IgM needs ≥2 of 3, IgG ≥5 of 10; flagellin cross-reacts); “Negative serology rules out the rash being Lyme” (✓ early serology is often negative; erythema migrans plus exposure is a clinical diagnosis).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive IgM blot at eight weeks means active Lyme disease. No: after the first month, an IgM-only blot is not evidence of active disease.
Trap two: a single forty-one kilodalton band makes the blot positive. No: IgM needs two of three bands, IgG five of ten, and flagellin cross-reacts.
Trap three: a negative test rules out early Lyme disease. No: antibodies lag behind the rash, which is diagnosed clinically.

scenes.title: The month-one guest
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “IgM is the month-one guest: welcome in the first 30 days, suspicious if alone after that. IgG is the crowd that stays: it needs five of ten at the door. IgM needs a pair: two of three.” Tokens: IgM = month one · IgM pair = 2 of 3 · IgG crowd = 5 of 10. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: IgM is the month-one guest. Welcome in the first thirty days, suspicious if it turns up alone after that. IgM needs a pair, two of three bands. IgG is the crowd that stays, and needs five of ten.

Where it breaks: modified two-tier testing uses no bands at all; antibodies of both classes can persist for years after infection, so serology is not a test of cure; and very early in the rash phase, neither guest has arrived.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “EIA → blot: IgM ≥2 of 3 only in the first 30 days · IgG ≥5 of 10”, “Rash + exposure = clinical diagnosis · B. mayonii: high spirochetemia → blood PCR”.

cues.text: Lyme serology is a two-tier test whose immunoblot needs at least two of three IgM bands in the first month or five of ten IgG bands, and because antibodies lag, erythema migrans in an exposed patient is diagnosed clinically.

props.label: EIA → blot: IgM ≥ 2/3 only < 30 days · IgG ≥ 5/10
Rash + exposure = clinical dx · B. mayonii → blood PCR

explanation.what: Plain language: Lyme disease is usually confirmed by looking for the patient’s antibodies, in two steps: a sensitive screen, then a more specific check. Antibodies take time to appear, so early tests are often negative, and the early antibody type (IgM) only counts in the first month. Scientific terms: standard two-tier testing (STTT: EIA or IFA, then Western immunoblot), modified two-tier testing (MTTT: two EIAs), IgM and IgG immunoblot band criteria, OspC (23 kDa), flagellin (41 kDa), window period, erythema migrans (EM), spirochetemia, Borrelia mayonii.
explanation.why: The first-tier EIA is highly sensitive but produces some false positives; the reflex blot raises specificity. IgM appears first and IgG generally follows, and most patients have detectable IgG beyond 30 days, so an IgM-only response after the first month should not be taken as evidence of active disease and may be a false positive. During the first weeks the antibody response is still developing, so serology misses many patients with EM.
explanation.measure: Tier 1 positive or equivocal → reflex immunoblot. IgM blot positive: ≥2 of 3 bands (23, 39, 41 kDa), used only with symptoms <30 days. IgG blot positive: ≥5 of 10 bands (18, 23, 28, 30, 39, 41, 45, 58, 66, 93 kDa). STTT specificity >95%; acute-phase EM sensitivity about 30–40% in CDC-cited studies. EM in about 70–80% of patients, about 1 week after the bite (range about 3–32 days). B. mayonii: median blood DNA load about 180 times that of B. burgdorferi in the first six patients.
explanation.differs: STTT (EIA → blot) vs MTTT (EIA → second EIA, no blot; more sensitive early); IgM blot (first month only) vs IgG blot (any stage); B. burgdorferi (low, transient spirochetemia; classic EM) vs B. mayonii (high spirochetemia; diffuse macular rash in some patients, nausea or vomiting; blood PCR useful).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret an IgM-positive/IgG-negative blot by illness duration, count bands to call a blot positive, choose the next step for a patient with EM and negative serology, or recognise B. mayonii from high spirochetemia and atypical rash.

questions.stem: A patient with 6 weeks of migratory joint pain has a positive Lyme first-tier EIA, a positive IgM immunoblot and a negative IgG immunoblot. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Not evidence of active Lyme disease; an IgM-only blot after the first month may be a false positive
options.rationale: Correct. The IgM blot is used only for illness of less than 30 days; most patients have detectable IgG after that, so an isolated IgM result at 6 weeks should not be used as evidence of active disease.
Incorrect. Beyond a month, an IgM-only result should not be used as evidence of active disease.
Incorrect. Late disease is supported by a positive IgG blot, which is negative here.

options.text: Repeat the IgM blot monthly until it turns negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Antibodies can persist long after infection; serology is not a test of cure.

questions.stem: Under standard criteria, an IgG Western immunoblot for Lyme disease is positive when it shows:

options.text: At least 5 of the 10 specified bands
At least 2 of the 3 specified bands
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the IgM blot rule.
Incorrect. Flagellin antibody cross-reacts and is common in healthy people.

options.text: Any single band equal to the control band
options.rationale: Incorrect. Single bands are not a positive result; over-reading bands causes misdiagnosis.

questions.stem: An acutely ill Minnesota resident has high fever, a diffuse macular rash and vomiting after tick exposure. Lyme serology is negative. Which statement about Borrelia mayonii best fits?

options.text: It causes unusually high spirochetemia, so blood PCR can detect it before antibodies appear
options.rationale: Correct. Blood DNA loads were about 180 times those of B. burgdorferi in the first report.

options.text: It is transmitted by the lone star tick
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is carried by Ixodes scapularis, the blacklegged tick.

options.text: It always produces a classic bull’s-eye rash
options.rationale: Incorrect. Rashes ranged from diffuse macular to a single lesion.

options.text: It has only ever been found in Minnesota
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cases were from Minnesota, Wisconsin and North Dakota, and a locally acquired case was reported in New York in 2025.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 61 Hit 8 gives standard two-tier sensitivity in early disease as ~40–60%. The CDC review (Moore 2016) gives 30–40% early (standard two-tier acute-phase table values 38–42%, convalescent 26–61%), and Branda 2021 cites 14% in solitary EM; figures depend on assay, stage and sampling time (register flag rv-lyme-early-sensitivity).

Ch. 61 Hit 8 presents the standard EIA → immunoblot algorithm as the standard without noting that CDC has accepted FDA-cleared modified two-tier (two-EIA) testing since 2019 (Mead 2019) (register flag rv-lyme-mttt-alternative).
Ch. 61 Hit 14 places B. mayonii in the upper Midwest; a locally acquired human case with infected local ticks was reported in New York in 2025 (Nafiz 2026) (register flag rv-mayonii-range).

Ch. 61 Hit 9 states the tick must feed >24–48 h to transmit efficiently. Cook 2015 argues the minimum attachment time is not established; the claim is kept pending and not taught (register flag rv-lyme-tick-attachment).
The testing algorithms taught are US (CDC/FDA) recommendations; European and Philippine practice is not covered, and MTLE candidates should check local guidance.
